title: The Dinner
blurb: It's Gran's birthday and the family come for dinner at seven — but Gran is ill upstairs, and tonight the cooking is all yours. With a takeaway man offering an easy cheat and the clock running down, you have two hours to get a good evening onto the table, and to decide who you let through the door.

identity.name: Dinner at Seven
identity.mood: A warm kitchen on a winter evening; dinner for the people you love, and two hours to get it right.

cover.alt: A warm, lit kitchen window on a dark winter street at night: steam on the glass, a pot on the hob and a table laid for dinner inside.

line.en: The family come for dinner at seven, and tonight the cooking is all yours. Get a good evening onto the table.
line.fr: La famille vient dîner à sept heures, et ce soir, c'est toi qui cuisines. Prépare une belle soirée à table.
line.es: La familia viene a cenar a las siete, y esta noche cocinas tú. Pon una buena velada en la mesa.
line.it: La famiglia viene a cena alle sette, e stasera cucini tu. Porta in tavola una bella serata.
line.de: Die Familie kommt um sieben zum Essen, und heute Abend kochst du. Bring einen schönen Abend auf den Tisch.
line.pt: A família vem jantar às sete, e esta noite quem cozinha és tu. Põe uma boa noite na mesa.
line.ru: Семья придёт на ужин в семь, и сегодня готовишь ты. Накрой хороший вечер на стол.
line.zh: 家人七点来吃晚饭，今晚做饭全靠你了。为大家张罗一桌好饭、一个好夜晚。
line.ar: تأتي العائلة للعشاء في السابعة، والليلة الطبخ كله عليك. قدِّم أمسية جميلة على المائدة.

hero.sub: A story where you are the hero — and every choice turns you to a new page. Written for people learning English, at your level, with meaning in your language whenever you need it.

B1: the first conditional and modals of advice
B2: hospitality, pride and letting people in

text.A2: It is five o'clock. The family come for dinner at seven. But Gran Ivy is ill in bed upstairs, and tonight she can't cook. The chicken is still in the fridge. The cake is half made. The table is bare. Getting a good dinner on the table is on you now.
text.B1: It is five o'clock, and the family come for dinner at seven. But Gran Ivy, who cooks this dinner every year, is ill in bed upstairs. The chicken is still in the fridge, the cake is half made, and the table is bare. For the first time, getting dinner on the table is all on you.
text.B2: It is five o'clock, and the whole family come for dinner at seven. But Gran Ivy, who has cooked this dinner for thirty years, is ill in bed upstairs and can't come down. The chicken is still in the fridge, the cake is only half made, and the table is bare. For the first time, getting a good dinner on the table is all on you.

text.A2: You see what the kitchen holds. There is a chicken, potatoes, flour, and butter. There is a big pan and a good oven. The clock is already at five. You have to decide what to do, and start soon.
text.B1: You see what the kitchen holds: a chicken, potatoes, flour, butter, a big pan, a good oven. The clock is already past five, and the room smells of nothing cooking. You have to decide what to do, and start soon.
text.B2: You take stock of what the kitchen holds: a chicken, a bag of potatoes, flour and butter, a big roasting pan, a good oven. The clock is already past five, and there's that quiet, empty feeling of a kitchen where nothing is cooking yet. You have to decide what to do, and you have to start soon.

text.A2: You call your mum to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings. At last she answers. She can't come over tonight, she says. She is too far away. But she talks you through Gran's recipe, step by step. 'You can do this,' she says.
text.B1: You call your mum to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings, then at last she answers. She can't come over tonight — she's too far away to help. But she talks you through Gran's recipe, step by step. 'You can do this,' she says, and somehow you start to believe her.
text.B2: You call your mum to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings, and then at last she answers. She can't come over tonight — she's an hour away, and the buses have stopped. But she talks you calmly through Gran's recipe, step by step, down the crackly line. 'You can do this,' she says, and somehow you start to believe her.

text.A2: You go up to Gran first. You bring her tea and make her warm. But the kitchen is still cold and empty. Being kind to Gran is good. But the dinner still needs cooking. You need a plan, and a clear head, before seven.
text.B1: You go up to Gran first. You bring her tea and make her comfortable. But the kitchen is still cold and empty downstairs. Sitting with Gran won't cook the dinner. The family will be hungry at seven. You need the shopping, a plan, and a clear head before you start.
text.B2: You go up to Gran first, bringing her tea and making her comfortable in bed. But the kitchen is still cold and empty downstairs, and sitting with Gran won't get the dinner cooked. The family will be at the door at seven, hungry and happy. You need the shopping, a plan, and a clear head before you can give them that.

text.A2: Feel how little time there is.
text.B1: Feel how little time there is.
text.B2: Feel how little time there is.

text.A2: You roll up your sleeves in the kitchen. The oven hums as it warms. Outside, the street is dark and wet. Then there is a knock at the gate — soft, once, then nothing. Someone is out there in the dark. But you weren't expecting anyone yet.
text.B1: You roll up your sleeves and get into the kitchen. The oven hums as it warms, and the window begins to steam. Outside, the street is dark and wet. Then you hear it: a knock at the gate — soft, once, then nothing. Someone is out there in the dark, and you weren't expecting anyone this early.
text.B2: You roll up your sleeves and get into the kitchen. The oven hums as it warms, and the window begins to steam up against the cold. Outside, the street is dark and wet and empty. Then you hear it: a knock at the gate — soft, just once, then nothing. Someone is out there in the dark tonight, and you weren't expecting a soul this early.

text.A2: You stop and think. You could start cooking right now. You could go up to Gran and the family first. Or you could call friends to come and help. Each choice costs time you do not have. And the clock keeps moving toward seven.
text.B1: You make yourself stop and think. You could start the cooking right now and sort the rest later. You could go to Gran and get things straight first. Or you could call a few friends to come and help. Each choice costs time you don't have — and the clock keeps moving toward seven.
text.B2: You make yourself stop and think it through. You could start the cooking right now and worry about everything else after. You could go up to Gran and the family and get things straight first. Or you could call a few friends and get more hands in the kitchen. Each choice costs time you don't have — and the clock keeps ticking, steadily, toward seven.

text.A2: The time presses on you like a weight. You think of the family at seven: the kids, the aunts, Gran's friends from the street. A whole evening, and it rests on you. That is not a worry; it is a plain fact. No one else is going to cook it. It is you, tonight, or no one.
text.B1: The time presses on you like a weight. You think of the family coming at seven — the kids, the aunts, Gran's old friends from the street — all of them hungry and happy. A whole evening rests on you now. That isn't a worry; it's a plain fact. No one else is going to cook it. It is you, tonight, or no one.
text.B2: The time presses on you like a weight. You think of the family coming at seven — the kids, the aunts, Gran's old friends from down the street — all of them hungry and happy and expecting her roast. A whole evening rests on you now. That isn't a worry; it's a plain fact. No one else is going to step in and cook it. It is you, tonight, or it is no one.

text.A2: You get straight into the cooking. You turn on the hob, put a pan on, cut a few things. But you have no proper plan. Half the food is still in the bags. This will not come together on its own. You can't just throw things in a pan and hope.
text.B1: You get straight into the cooking. You turn on the hob, put a pan on, start cutting. But you've no proper plan, and half the food is still in the bags. Rushing like this, it won't come together on its own. You can't just throw things in a pan and hope for the best.
text.B2: You get straight into the cooking. You turn on the hob, slap a pan down, start cutting whatever's to hand. But you've no proper plan, and half the food is still sitting in the shopping bags. Rushed like this, it won't come together on its own. You can't just throw things in a pan and hope the evening turns out well.

text.A2: You take charge of the food and the recipe. You lay it all out on the table: chicken, potatoes, butter, the cake things. Done well, this makes a real dinner for seven. Rushed and wasted, and there's nothing on the table. So you start, carefully.
text.B1: You take charge of the food and Gran's recipe. You lay it all out on the table — chicken, potatoes, butter, the things for the cake. Done well, this makes a real dinner for seven. Rushed or wasted, and the table stays bare. So you take a breath and start, carefully.
text.B2: You take charge of the food and Gran's recipe. You lay it all out along the table — the chicken, the bag of potatoes, the butter, the things for the cake. Done properly, this is a real dinner for the whole family at seven. Rushed or wasted, and the table stays bare. So you take a breath, and you start, carefully.

text.A2: Ask Joan next door for tips.
text.B1: Ask Joan next door for tips.
text.B2: Ask Joan next door for tips.

text.A2: You grab just a pan and a knife and start. They let you begin, and that feels good. But it is not a plan, and you've bought nothing extra. You'll still need the shopping, and soon. If not, there won't be enough for seven.
text.B1: You grab just a pan and a knife and make a start. They let you begin, and that feels like something. But it isn't a plan, and you've bought nothing extra. You'll still need the shopping, and soon. If not, there won't be enough for everyone at seven.
text.B2: You grab just a pan and a knife and make a start. They let you begin, and that feels like something, at least. But it isn't a plan, and you've bought nothing extra for the table. You'll still need to get the shopping, and soon. Without it, there simply won't be enough to go round at seven.

text.A2: Ask Joan next door for tips.
text.B1: Ask Joan next door for tips.
text.B2: Ask Joan next door for tips.

text.A2: Old Joan next door has cooked a thousand dinners. 'Don't run across the main road,' she says. 'It saves ten minutes. It's not worth it in the dark.' She warns you about Dale too, from the takeaway. 'Cook your own food. Watch the oven. That's the whole job tonight.'
text.B1: Old Joan next door has cooked a thousand dinners in her time. 'Don't run across the main road,' she says. 'It saves ten minutes — and it's not worth it in the dark and the rain.' She warns you about Dale too, from the takeaway. 'Cook your own food, keep an eye on the oven. That's the whole job tonight.'
text.B2: Old Joan next door has cooked a thousand dinners in her time, and she knows a panic when she sees one. 'Don't run across the main road,' she says. 'It saves you ten minutes — and it's not worth it, not in the dark and the rain.' She warns you about Dale as well, the fellow from the takeaway. 'Cook your own food, and keep one eye on the oven. That's the whole job tonight.'

text.A2: You help your neighbour, Mr Doyle, who is locked out in the cold. You get him inside and sit him down with tea. Little by little, he warms up. 'Bless you,' he says, holding your hand. You promise to pop back later. Then you go back to your kitchen and the clock.
text.B1: You help your neighbour, Mr Doyle, who's locked out of his flat in the cold. You get him inside and sit him down with a cup of tea. Little by little, he warms up and stops shivering. 'Bless you,' he says, gripping your hand. You promise to look in on him later, then go back to your own kitchen and the clock.
text.B2: You help your neighbour, Mr Doyle, who's locked out of his flat and shivering on the step. You get him inside, sit him down, and put the kettle on. Little by little he warms up and the colour comes back to his face. 'Bless you,' he says, gripping your hand. You promise to look in on him later, then turn back to your own kitchen and the ticking clock.

text.A2: He asks you to check the others.
text.B1: He asks you to check the others.
text.B2: He asks you to check the others.

text.A2: The cooking comes first. The rest can wait a moment. But you still have to choose how. You could go to the shop for what you need first. Or you could start with what you've got and sort it as you go.
text.B1: The cooking comes first. The rest can wait a moment. But you still have to choose how. You could go to the shop for what you need first. Or you could start with what you've got and sort the rest as you go.
text.B2: Getting the cooking going comes first; the rest can wait a moment. But you still have to choose how to do it. You could go to the shop for what you need and set yourself up properly. Or you could start with what you've already got, and sort the rest out as you go along.

text.A2: The rush catches up with you. Your back aches, your hands shake, and the clock keeps moving. You are doing too much at once, and you know it. If you tire yourself out now, nothing gets finished. So slow down, and do one thing at a time.
text.B1: The rush catches up with you. Your back aches, your hands are shaking, and the clock won't stop. You're trying to do too much at once, and you know it. If you tire yourself out now, nothing gets finished. So slow down, and do one thing at a time.
text.B2: The rush catches up with you all at once. Your back aches, your hands are shaking, and the clock on the wall will not stop moving. You're trying to do far too much at once, and you know it. If you burn yourself out now, nothing gets finished at all. So slow down, breathe, and do one thing at a time.

text.A2: You call round, and friends start to come. One brings a dish. One brings chairs. Another just rolls up their sleeves. Bit by bit, a plan takes shape. You are not doing this alone any more. And that changes everything.
text.B1: You call round, and friends start to arrive. One brings a dish of their own. One brings extra chairs. Another just rolls up their sleeves and asks what to chop. Bit by bit, a plan takes shape. You're not doing this alone any more — and that changes everything.
text.B2: You call round, and friends start to arrive at the door. One brings a dish of their own to add to the table. One brings extra chairs under both arms. Another just rolls up their sleeves and asks what needs chopping. Bit by bit, hand by hand, a plan takes shape in the warm kitchen. You're not doing this alone any more — and that, more than anything, changes the evening.

text.A2: No one can come. One is working, one is out, one just doesn't pick up. You can't make them. So you turn back to the kitchen and go on alone. It is harder this way. But the family still come at seven.
text.B1: No one can come. One is working late, one is already out, one just doesn't pick up the phone. You can't make them. So you turn back to the kitchen and go on alone. It's harder this way. But the family still come at seven, ready or not.
text.B2: No one can come, in the end. One is working late, one is already out for the evening, one simply doesn't pick up. You can't make anyone help you. So you turn back to the kitchen and go on alone; it's harder this way, dish by dish — but the family still come at seven, ready or not.

text.A2: The first dishes are on. Now you need a few things from the shop. There are two ways there. The long way round the block is safe but slow. Straight across the main road is quick. But it's dark and wet, and cars come fast.
text.B1: The first dishes are on. Now you need a few things from the shop to finish. There are two ways there. The long way round the block is safe but slow. Straight across the main road is quick. But it's dark and wet, and the cars come fast.
text.B2: The first dishes are on and ticking over. Now you need a few last things from the shop to finish the meal. There are two ways to get there: the long way round the block, safe but slow, or straight across the main road, quick and tempting. But it's dark and wet out, and the cars come fast along that road.

text.A2: You take old Joan's words to heart. Cook your own food. Watch the oven. Don't trust Dale. And stay off that main road. It is simple advice, and good. Now you just have to follow it.
text.B1: You take old Joan's words to heart. Cook your own food. Keep an eye on the oven. Don't trust Dale. And stay well off that main road. It's simple advice, and good. Now you just have to follow it, with the clock running.
text.B2: You take old Joan's words to heart, one by one. Cook your own food. Keep one eye on the oven. Don't trust a word Dale says. And stay well off that main road in the dark. It's simple advice, and good — the hard part is following it when you're tired and the clock is running down.

text.A2: You feel better for helping someone. Oddly, it steadies you too. Your head is clearer, and your hands are surer. There's still a lot to do before seven. But now you feel able to do it.
text.B1: You feel better for the good turn you did. Helping someone, oddly, seems to steady you too. Your head is clearer, and your hands are surer. There's still a lot to do before seven. But now you feel able to meet it.
text.B2: You feel better for the good turn you did. Helping someone out, oddly enough, seems to steady you as well. Your head is clearer now, and your hands are surer on the work. There's still a great deal to do before seven — but you feel, for the first time since Gran called down, able to meet it.

text.A2: Dale from the takeaway is at the door, all smiles. He has hot food in bags and an easy way out. 'Why cook, love?' he says. 'Buy mine, tip it in your dishes. No one will ever know.' You've heard that kind of thing before.
text.B1: Dale from the takeaway is at the door, all smiles. He has hot food in bags and an easy way out to sell you. 'Why go to all that trouble, love?' he says. 'Buy mine, tip it into your own dishes — no one will ever know.' You've heard that kind of offer before.
text.B2: Dale from the takeaway on the corner is at your door, all smiles, steam rising off the bags in his hands. He has hot food to sell and an easy way out to go with it. 'Why go to all that trouble, love?' he says. 'Buy mine, tip it into your own dishes — no one will ever know the difference.' You've heard that kind of offer before, and you know a hook when it's dangled.

text.A2: You get everyone busy in the kitchen. Working together, it all feels lighter. One peels, one stirs, one lays the table. 'This bit next,' you say, and they follow. It's a good feeling, with the clock running.
text.B1: You get everyone busy in the kitchen. Working together, the whole thing feels lighter. One peels the potatoes, one stirs a pot, one lays the table. 'This bit next,' you say, and they follow your lead. It's a good feeling, with the clock running down.
text.B2: You get everyone busy in the warm kitchen. Working together, the whole evening suddenly feels lighter than it did. One peels the potatoes, one stirs a pot, one lays the table under your eye. 'This bit next,' you say, and they follow your lead. It's a good feeling to have, with the clock running down toward seven.

text.A2: The knock at the gate again.
text.B1: The knock at the gate again.
text.B2: The knock at the gate again.

text.A2: The long way round is dark and cold. The rain is on your face, and there is no shelter. But it is safe under your feet, and it gets you to the shop. So you keep walking, as fast as you dare.
text.B1: The long way round is dark and cold, the rain on your face, no shelter at all. But it's safe under your feet, and it gets you to the shop and back. So you keep walking, as fast as you dare, step after step.
text.B2: The long way round the block is dark and cold, the rain stinging your face, with no shelter at all along the way. But it's safe under your feet, and it gets you to the shop and back in one piece. So you keep walking into it, as fast as you dare, step after step after step.

text.A2: The quiet street, all lit windows.
text.B1: The quiet street, all lit windows.
text.B2: The quiet street, all lit windows.

text.A2: You step out into the main road, and at once it feels wrong. The cars come fast out of the dark and rain. Every step is a gamble now. And there is no going back once you are out in the traffic.
text.B1: You step out into the main road, and at once it feels wrong. The cars come fast out of the dark and the rain, their lights in your eyes. Every step is a gamble now — and there's no going back once you're out in the traffic.
text.B2: You step out into the main road, and at once it feels wrong. The cars come fast out of the dark and the rain, headlights swinging straight into your eyes. Every single step is a gamble now — and there's no going back once you're out in the middle of the traffic.

text.A2: A car comes out of nowhere.
text.B1: A car comes out of nowhere.
text.B2: A car comes out of nowhere.

text.A2: The oven clicks and clicks but won't light. The gas must be low. You can cook on the hob, but it is slow, and there is a lot to do. You'll have to make do. Or nip to the shop and sort it there.
text.B1: The oven clicks and clicks but won't light — the gas must be low. You can still cook on the hob, but it's slow, and there's a lot to get through. You'll have to make do with it. Or nip down to the shop and sort it out there.
text.B2: The oven clicks and clicks but won't light — the gas must be running low. You can still cook on the hob, but it's slow going, and there's a great deal to get through before seven. You'll have to make do with it — or nip down to the corner shop and sort it out there.

text.A2: To the shop — sort it there.
text.B1: To the shop — sort it there.
text.B2: To the shop — sort it there.

text.A2: The street runs on, cold and wet, the rain coming harder. One house sits dark, with no one home. Ahead, the wind pushes at you. And there is a shop sign at the corner, half torn down in the rain.
text.B1: The street runs on, cold and wet, the rain coming harder by the minute. One house sits dark, with no one home. Ahead, the wind pushes back at you. And there's a shop sign at the corner, half torn down in the rain.
text.B2: The street runs on, cold and wet, the rain coming harder by the minute now. One house sits dark along it, with no lights and no one home. Ahead, the wind pushes back at you with every step. And there's a shop sign at the corner, half torn down and swinging in the rain.

text.A2: An old man has slipped on the wet pavement and can't get up. The cold is getting into him. Stop, and you lose time you don't have. Don't, and he could be there a while.
text.B1: An old man has slipped on the wet pavement and can't get up. The cold is getting into him fast. Stop, and you lose time you don't have. Don't, and he could be stuck there a long while in the rain.
text.B2: An old man has slipped on the wet pavement and can't get himself up. The cold is getting into him fast, there on the ground. Stop, and you lose time you don't have; don't, and he could be stuck there a long while in the rain, with no one else about.

text.A2: You hurry on through the cold and the rain, head down. Choices lie ahead. Dale may be near. There is that knock at the gate. Or you can just get on with the dinner.
text.B1: You hurry on through the cold and the rain, head down against it. Choices lie ahead. Dale may be near. There's that soft knock at the gate to think about. Or you can just get on with the dinner.
text.B2: You hurry on through the cold and the rain, head down against the worst of it. Choices lie ahead of you in the dark. Dale may be near with his bags. There's that soft knock at the gate still to think about. Or you can simply get on with the dinner and the clock.

text.A2: You help the old man up and walk him to his door. His eyes fill. He presses a bag into your hands — fresh herbs from his window box. 'Take them,' he says, 'for the dinner.' A small thing, freely given. You take it and go on.
text.B1: You help the old man up and walk him to his door. His eyes fill. He presses a small bag into your hands — fresh herbs from his window box. 'Take them,' he says, 'for your dinner.' A small thing — but freely given, and you take it and go on.
text.B2: You help the old man up and walk him safely to his door. His eyes fill, and he presses a small paper bag into your hands — fresh herbs from his window box. 'Take them,' he says, 'for your dinner.' A small thing — but freely given, in the rain, and you take it and go on your way.

text.A2: He tells you about the knock at your gate.
text.B1: He tells you about the knock at your gate.
text.B2: He tells you about the knock at your gate.

text.A2: You can't stop now. But you can't just leave them, either. So you promise to send help round soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay warm, stay put — I won't forget you.' You mean it, too. And then you go.
text.B1: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave them, either. So you promise to send help round soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay warm, stay put — I won't forget you.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and go.
text.B2: You can't stop now — but you can't simply leave them, either. So you promise to send help round soon. 'Hang on,' you say, over the rain. 'Stay warm, stay put — I won't forget you.' You mean it, too; and then you turn and go, carrying the weight of it with you.

text.A2: You and the friends get one big pot going — a warm stew that will feed everyone. People gather round the warm hob. It is not the whole dinner. But it is real food, and a start.
text.B1: You and the friends get one big pot going — a warm stew that will feed everyone, whatever else happens. People gather round the warm hob. It isn't the whole dinner. But it's real food, and a good beginning.
text.B2: You and the friends get one big pot going — a warm, simple stew that will feed everyone, whatever else happens with the clock. People gather round the warm hob, glad of it. It isn't the whole dinner, not by a long way. But it's real food, and a good beginning, and the kitchen smells of it.

text.A2: Friend by friend, the panic turns into a working kitchen. People have jobs now: one peels, one stirs, one lays the table. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The kitchen fills up with noise and warmth.
text.B1: Friend by friend, the panic turns into a working kitchen. People have jobs now: one peels, one stirs, one lays the table. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The kitchen fills up with noise and warmth.
text.B2: Friend by friend, task by task, the panic turns into a working kitchen. People have jobs now: one peels the potatoes, one stirs a pot, one lays the table under your eye. Worry turns into doing — and doing beats worrying, in a kitchen, every single time. The kitchen fills up with noise and warmth, and the worst of the panic lifts.

text.A2: To the shop for the rest.
text.B1: To the shop for the rest.
text.B2: To the shop for the rest.

text.A2: The long evening wears at you. A voice says: give up, order a takeaway, put your feet up. No one would blame you, and it would be easy. But you think of Gran's face at a full table. And you push the voice away. Not yet.
text.B1: The long evening wears at you. A small voice says: give up, order a takeaway, put your feet up — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy. But you think of Gran's face at a full table. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while it can still be good.
text.B2: The long evening wears at you. A small voice says: give up, order a takeaway, put your feet up — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy to do. But you think of Gran's face coming down to a full, warm table. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while the evening can still be good.

text.A2: You stop under a lamp to read the rest of Gran's list. Half of it is smudged by the rain. You could push on to the shop for the rest. Or something makes you look back at the gate, and that soft knock.
text.B1: You stop under a street lamp to read the rest of Gran's list. Half of it is smudged by the rain. You could push on to the shop and get the rest. Or something makes you look back at the gate, and that soft knock you heard.
text.B2: You stop under a street lamp to read the rest of Gran's list, but half of it is smudged and run by the rain. You could push on to the shop and get the last few things. Or something makes you look back, down the dark street, toward the gate and that soft knock you heard earlier.

text.A2: Dale leans in close, all friendly. 'Cold out here,' he says. 'I've got the lot — chicken, spuds, all hot. Tip it in your dishes, no one knows. Why make trouble for yourself?' His smile is wide. But his eyes don't smile with it.
text.B1: Dale leans in close, all friendly. 'Cold out here,' he says. 'I've got the lot — chicken, spuds, all hot and ready. Tip it into your dishes, and no one's any the wiser. Why make all this trouble for yourself?' His smile is wide. But his eyes don't smile with it.
text.B2: Dale leans in close, all friendly. 'Cold out here,' he says. 'I've got the lot — chicken, spuds, all hot and ready to go. Tip it into your own dishes, and no one's ever any the wiser. Why make all this trouble for yourself, love?' His smile is wide and easy. But his eyes don't smile along with it, and you notice that.

text.A2: 'Fair price,' Dale says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot. But he's quick, he's hot, and he's right here. No shop, no cooking, no mess. So: pay him, turn him down, or ask him straight what his game is?
text.B1: 'Fair price,' Dale says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot of money. But he's quick, he's hot, and he's right here in front of you. No shop, no cooking, no mess to clear up. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down, or ask what his game is?
text.B2: 'Fair price,' Dale says, and names a sum that makes you blink in the rain. It's a lot of money, more than the shop would ever charge. But he's quick, he's hot, and he's right here in front of you now. No shop, no cooking, no mess to clear up after. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down flat, or ask him straight out what his game really is?

text.A2: You say no thanks and walk on. It feels good to turn him down. He calls after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone. But it won't be you, not tonight.
text.B1: You say no thanks and walk on past him. It feels good to turn him down. He calls something after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone, in the end. But it won't be you, not tonight.
text.B2: You say no thanks and walk on past him into the rain. It feels good to turn him down flat. He calls something after you, but you don't look back. His sort always find someone, in the end — someone tired and frightened enough. But it won't be you, not tonight.

text.A2: You take his food and hand over the money. Your hands close on the warm bags, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart. It feels like a small lie starting.
text.B1: You take his food and hand over the money. Your hands close on the warm bags, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels like a small lie, just starting.
text.B2: You take his food and hand over the money. Your hands close on the warm bags, and part of you already knows the truth of it. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels, in the cold, like a small lie being told — one you'll have to keep telling all evening.

text.A2: You ask him straight: why so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'A flop tonight, and you'll be back to mine next week.' He's honest, at least. That tells you all you need to know.
text.B1: You ask him straight: why is he so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'A flop tonight, and you'll be back to mine next week.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that tells you all you need to know.
text.B2: You ask him straight out: why is he so keen to help? He laughs, quite openly. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'And if your dinner's a flop tonight, you'll be back to mine next week, won't you.' At least he's honest about it — and that, right there, tells you everything you need to know.

text.A2: You tip his food into your own dishes. But up close it looks wrong — greasy, grey, nothing like Gran's. It won't fool anyone at the table. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B1: You tip his food into your own dishes. But up close it looks all wrong — greasy, grey, nothing like Gran's cooking. It won't fool anyone at the table for a second. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B2: You tip his food into your own dishes and try to make it look like yours. But up close it looks all wrong — greasy, grey, and nothing at all like Gran's cooking. It won't fool anyone at that table for a second. And the whole thing already feels, in your stomach, like a mistake.

text.A2: You open the bag, and the smell hits you — cold grease, old fat, nothing fresh. This food won't pass for home cooking. You paid good money, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right.
text.B1: You open the bag, and the smell hits you — cold grease, old fat, nothing fresh about it. This food will never pass for home cooking. You paid good money for it, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right all along.
text.B2: You open the bag, and the smell hits you — cold grease, old fat, nothing fresh about any of it. This food will never pass for home cooking, not at Gran's table. You paid good money for it, out here in the rain, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right about him all along.

text.A2: You turn to find Dale, but he's already gone, off into the rain. He was never really helping. He just wanted the sale, and a flop tonight so you'd come back. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B1: You turn to find Dale, but he's already gone, off into the rain. He was never really helping you. He just wanted the sale — and a flop tonight, so you'd come back to him. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B2: You turn to find Dale, but he's already gone, melted off into the rain. He was never really helping you at all. He just wanted the sale — and a flop tonight, so you'd be back at his counter next week. You've been had, out here, plain and simple. The rain keeps on, and the money's gone with him.

text.A2: He's gone, and the street is empty. Just the rain now, and the money you gave him for nothing. You learned something tonight. And you paid too much for it. Now you go on with less than you had.
text.B1: He's gone, and the street is empty — just the rain now, and the money you handed him for nothing. You learned something tonight. And you paid far too much for it. Now you go on with less than you started with.
text.B2: He's gone, and the street is empty — just the rain now, the dark, and the money you handed him for nothing at all. You learned something tonight, out here. And you paid far too much for it. Now you go on with less than you started with, and the clock no kinder.

text.A2: Stand a moment in the rain.
text.B1: Stand a moment in the rain.
text.B2: Stand a moment in the rain.

text.A2: Other tired people are buying from Dale too, hands full of money, glad of the easy way. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only helps the ones who pay the most.
text.B1: Other tired people are buying from Dale too — hands full of money, glad of the easy way out. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay the most.
text.B2: Other tired people are buying from Dale too — hands full of money, glad of any easy way out tonight. He takes it slow, unhurried, with that same wide smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay him the most — and you see the whole of him in it.

text.A2: You're halfway across the main road now. The far side looks close — or does it? The rain and the headlights play tricks. And you are a long way from both kerbs.
text.B1: You're halfway across the main road now. The far side looks close — or does it? The rain and the headlights play tricks on your eyes. And you're a long way from both kerbs, out in the middle.
text.B2: You're halfway across the main road now, and the far side looks close — or does it? The rain and the swinging headlights play tricks on your tired eyes. And you're a long way from both kerbs, out in the middle of it, with the traffic coming. You keep your feet moving, and you do not look down.

text.A2: A car comes fast out of the dark, its lights filling your eyes. This is the moment. You can keep going and hope it stops. Or you can jump back to the kerb, while you still can.
text.B1: A car comes fast out of the dark, its lights filling your eyes, its horn blaring. This is the moment. You can keep going and hope it stops in time. Or you can jump back to the kerb, while you still can.
text.B2: A car comes fast out of the dark, its lights filling your eyes, its horn blaring over the rain. This is the moment, and it's a short one. You can keep going and hope it stops in time. Or you can throw yourself back toward the kerb, right now, while you still can.

text.A2: You reach the far side at last, soaked and shaking — but across. Somehow you made it. Now you must choose. Push on, shaken as you are? Or go back for what you dropped in the road?
text.B1: You reach the far side at last, soaked and shaking, your heart going hard — but across. Somehow you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, shaken as you are, or go back for what you dropped in the road.
text.B2: You reach the far side at last, soaked and shaking, your heart going hard against your ribs — but across. Somehow, against the odds, you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, shaken as you are, or go back for the shopping you dropped out there in the road.

text.A2: You jump back to the kerb just in time — the right, hard choice. The car roars past, close enough to feel. You stand there shaking, but safe. The night isn't lost. But you've lost time, and you'll go round now.
text.B1: You jump back to the kerb just in time — the hard, right choice. The car roars past, close enough to feel the wind of it. You stand there shaking, but safe. The night isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll miss — and you'll go the long way now.
text.B2: You throw yourself back to the kerb just in time — the hard choice, and the right one. The car roars past, close enough to feel the wind of it on your face. You stand there shaking, but safe. The night isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll badly miss — and you'll go the long way round now, like you should have.

text.A2: You try to help with their dinner. Put a pan on, find what's in the cupboard, get something warm going. It helps a little. But they've next to nothing in, and you can't stay long. There's only one real thing you can do.
text.B1: You try to help with their dinner — put a pan on, see what's in the cupboard, get something warm started. It helps a little. But they've next to nothing in the house, and you can't stay long. There's really only one thing you can do for them.
text.B2: You try to help with their dinner — put a pan on, see what's in the near-empty cupboard, get something warm started for the kids. It helps a little. But they've next to nothing in the house, and you can't stay long tonight. There's really only one thing left that you can do for them.

text.A2: You hand over your own bags of food, and the family's faces change. The kids crowd round the table. The little one stops crying. 'Thank you,' the mum says — then she tells you someone's waiting at your gate.
text.B1: You hand over your own bags of food, and the family's faces change. The kids crowd round the table at the thought of a hot meal. The little one stops crying at last. 'Thank you,' the mum says — and then she tells you someone's been waiting at your gate.
text.B2: You hand over your own bags of food, and the family's tired faces change all at once. The kids crowd round the table at the thought of a hot meal. The little one stops crying at last. 'Thank you,' the mum says, over and over — and then she tells you someone's been waiting at your gate, in the rain.

text.A2: With your own food given away, your heart sinks a little. Now there's less for your own table. You gave it to help, and you'd do it again. But the clock doesn't care about that. It just keeps ticking.
text.B1: With your own food given away, your heart sinks a little. Now there's less for your own table at seven. You gave it to help, and you'd do it again. But the clock doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps ticking on.
text.B2: With your own food given away, your heart sinks a little in your chest. Now there's that much less for your own table at seven. You gave it away to help, and you'd do it again in a heartbeat. But the clock on the wall doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps ticking on toward the hour.

text.A2: A warm café offers a sit-down.
text.B1: A warm café offers a sit-down.
text.B2: A warm café offers a sit-down.

text.A2: A neighbour waves you into a warm café. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cuppa.' It's warm in there. Your tired feet beg you to stop. But five minutes can turn into twenty.
text.B1: A neighbour waves you into a warm café. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cup of tea.' It's warm and dry inside, and your tired feet beg you to stop. But five minutes like this can quietly turn into twenty.
text.B2: A neighbour waves you into a warm, bright café out of the rain. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, dry off, have a cup of tea.' It's warm and dry in there, and your cold, tired feet beg you to stop. But five minutes like this one can quietly turn into twenty, with the clock running.

text.A2: You press on through the rain, cold and wet. Your bags are heavy, the clock in your head. Each step is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward home and the kitchen.
text.B1: You press on through the rain, cold and wet, your bags heavy, the clock ticking in your head. Each step is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward home and the warm kitchen.
text.B2: You press on through the rain, cold and wet to the skin, your bags heavy in your hands and the clock ticking loud in your head. Each step is a small effort on its own now. But you keep them coming, one after another after another, toward home and the warm, waiting kitchen.
